_meta: DRAFT — NOT YET IMPORTED (wired automatically by the gen-slices auto-loader). Municipal-tier population-priority push, 2026-08-13 (AF/G.18), round 20 of 20 (Wave D) — the final country in this 20-round push. Zimbabwe — 26th-highest-population country. `zw-zimstat-cpi` already covers CPI; this round adds the constitutional devolution-fund mechanism (Section 301, a 5% minimum) and the local-authority fiscal tier. Zimbabwe's own Auditor-General publishes a rich, continuous named-council audit series (structurally the same document type found this round for Malawi, Zambia, and Senegal, and in earlier rounds for Nigeria and Côte d'Ivoire) — a document type now confirmed repeatable across at least seven otherwise-unrelated African countries' supreme audit institutions.

reports.title: Constitution of Zimbabwe (Amendment No. 20) Act, 2013 — Chapter 17, Section 301 (Allocation of revenues between provincial and local tiers of government)
reports.description: Zimbabwe's constitutional devolution mandate, verified via direct PDF download and pdftotext extraction (text-layer copy; a separate ILO NATLEX-hosted copy of the same Constitution is a non-OCR'd scan and could not independently confirm this quote). Sec. 301(3): "Not less than five per cent of the national revenues raised in any financial year must be allocated to the provinces and local authorities as their share in that year." This is the constitutional floor that Zimbabwe's annual devolution fund allocation (zw-budget-speech-2026) operationalizes.

reports.title: Urban Councils Act [Chapter 29:15], Zimbabwe
reports.description: Zimbabwe's organic law governing urban local authorities, verified via direct PDF download and pdftotext extraction. Sec. 272(1): "as often as it considers necessary in respect of each financial year or part thereof, a council may fix and levy a general rate upon all rateable property in the council area." Sec. 273(1): a council may "fix and levy a special rate upon all rateable property in that portion of its area which derives benefit" from specific works, to recover the cost of those works. This is the legal basis the Auditor-General's own reporting confirms individual councils actually operate under (see zw-auditor-general-local-authorities-2023).

reports.title: 2026 National Budget Statement
reports.publisher: Ministry of Finance, Economic Development and Investment Promotion, Zimbabwe
reports.description: Zimbabwe's own Ministry of Finance operationalizing the constitutional devolution mandate, verified via direct PDF download and pdftotext extraction (line-confirmed). §74: "In addition, in compliance with sections 264 and 301 of the Constitution, which requires an allocation of at least 5% of revenue collections to the lower tiers of Government, a total of ZiG14.4 billion has been set aside for devolution and decentralisation in 2026." A separate, distinct line item (§73) allocates "ZiG4.6 billion...for the Ministry of Local Government and Public Works for the refurbishment and construction of Government buildings, disaster relief, as well as strengthening governance and oversight role of lower tiers of Government" — not part of the devolution fund itself. The Treasury's own "Approved 2026 Estimates of Expenditure" independently corroborates the figure under Vote VI (Local Government and Public Works): "Transfers to Provincial Councils and Local Authorities/Grant...14,382,000,000" for 2026 (2025 revised estimate: 13,614,000,000 ZiG), citing "Section 301(3) of Chapter 17 of the Constitution" as its authorizing basis — though that companion document could only be retrieved via a WebFetch rendering (direct curl was blocked by a Cloudflare JS challenge), so treat the Estimates figure as corroborating-but-not-independently-verified relative to the Budget Speech's own directly-confirmed text.
reports.cadence_note: Annual National Budget Statement; this is the FY2026 edition.

reports.title: Report of the Auditor-General on Local Authorities (2023 edition)
reports.publisher: Office of the Auditor-General of Zimbabwe
reports.description: Zimbabwe's Auditor-General reporting on named lower-tier units, verified via direct PDF download and pdftotext extraction (line-confirmed for each quote). Mutoko Rural District Council (audit year 2022): "The Council used ZWL$1.25 million from the devolution fund account to fund recurrent expenditure (salaries and wages). This was contrary to the Local Authorities Circular number 1 of 2019, which prohibits Council to use devolution funds as recurrent expenditure." Bulawayo City Council (2019 and 2020): "I have audited the financial statements of Bulawayo City Council for the years ended December 31, 2019 and 2020...The financial statements were prepared with reference to the Urban Councils Act [Chapter 29:15] and the Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19]" — with reported figures including "cumulative amount receivable from ZESA as at the reporting date was ZWL$798 million (2019: ZWL$208.2 million)." Mutare City Council (2022): audited on a consolidated basis with its subsidiary and issued "an adverse opinion...because of the significance of the matters discussed in the Basis for Adverse Opinion section" — no devolution-fund figure found in Mutare's specific section (searched, zero matches). A companion 2020 edition of the same report series adds Zvishavane Town Council ("Council intends to improve the sewer system through the recently introduced devolution funds") and Ruwa Local Board ("The council could also purchase the fire tender using devolution funds if the government approves").
reports.cadence_note: Annual Auditor-General report on local authorities; this file draws on both the 2023 and 2020 editions of a continuous series.

reports.title: City of Harare 2023 Consolidated Budget
reports.description: The City of Harare's own official site publishing budget figures. Revenue Classification table: total projected income for 2023 given as "134,787,687,460.00," rising to "213,427,117,500.04" when grants are included; property-tax billing at "63,679,641,116.00"; user/service charges at "42,304,938,473.80." A companion document, the City's proposed 2026 budget tariffs notice, gives itemized rate ranges (residential property rates "USD 4.50 to 90.00 per unit"; high-density water charges "0-5 cubic meters: USD 2.00"). CAVEAT: both documents were retrieved only via an AI-summarizing fetch tool, not independently re-verified against raw PDF text via direct download/pdftotext — flagged per this branch's standing practice for AI-summarized-only sourcing (cf. Ethiopia's Addis Ababa budget-announcement node). The currency unit for the 2023 figures (likely ZWL, given the period) was not explicitly confirmed in the retrieved summary.
reports.cadence_note: Annual city budget; this is the FY2023 consolidated edition, verification-limited per the caveat above.

dependencies.basis: The Budget Statement directly invokes the constitutional provision it is implementing: "In addition, in compliance with sections 264 and 301 of the Constitution, which requires an allocation of at least 5% of revenue collections to the lower tiers of Government, a total of ZiG14.4 billion has been set aside for devolution and decentralisation in 2026."

The Auditor-General's own Bulawayo City Council audit states directly that the council's "financial statements were prepared with reference to the Urban Councils Act [Chapter 29:15] and the Public Finance Management Act [Chapter 22:19]" — naming the Act as the council's own legal reporting basis.

_dropped.why: Three specific candidate URLs (a Chairman's Budget Speech, a full submission, and an amended 2025 tariff schedule) all failed with ROBOTS_DISALLOWED; one additionally reported an expired TLS certificate, suggesting a genuinely broken/misconfigured council server rather than a mere robots block. Document titles found via search confirm these files exist.

_dropped.edge: Mutare City Council's own site -> a self-published budget/financial-statement document
_dropped.why: No City-of-Mutare-hosted primary finance document was located at all after search — a genuine NOT FOUND, distinct from Bulawayo's case (where documents are known to exist but are inaccessible).

_dropped.edge: National Budget devolution fund -> a per-province or per-council breakdown annex
_dropped.why: Both the 2026 Budget Speech and the Approved 2026 Estimates of Expenditure give only a single aggregate national figure under one consolidated 'Transfers to Provincial Councils and Local Authorities' line item. This is recorded as an incomplete negative, not a confirmed absence: the Estimates of Expenditure PDF sits behind a Cloudflare JS challenge that defeated direct curl access, so a later annex with a province-by-province table may exist beyond what WebFetch's summarization surfaced — worth a follow-up session with browser-capable tooling.

_dropped.edge: ZIMSTAT's own CPI methodology -> COICOP (consistency across releases)
_dropped.why: ZIMSTAT's December 2023 CPI release explicitly names COICOP in its methodology section ("linking factors were proportions of estimated household expenditure in USD and ZWL according to the COICOP classification"), independently verified via direct download. However, the more recent December 2025 release is a short press-release-format document with NO methodology section at all (grep for COICOP/IMF/ILO/SADC returned zero matches) — ZIMSTAT's own methodology documentation is inconsistent across releases rather than absent outright, worth flagging as a documented inconsistency rather than either a full positive or full negative finding.

_dropped.edge: ILO NATLEX's own hosted copy of the Constitution -> independent verbatim confirmation of Section 301(3)
_dropped.why: The NATLEX copy (a fully official government-gazette-sourced document in principle) is a scanned image PDF with no OCR text layer — pdftotext produced zero usable characters, confirmed via pdfinfo showing a scanner-origin Creator field. The Veritas Zimbabwe text-layer copy was used instead for verbatim confirmation; both are believed to carry identical legal text, but only the Veritas copy could be independently quote-verified this round.
